policy: Review every closed candidate set. Select only when ASV wording or an explicit mapped textual note distinguishes a reading; otherwise mark underdetermined and retain the base fallback. The base candidate is the SBLGNT reading.

decisions.evidence: ASV punctuates the apostle pairs with a semicolon ('Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee'), and English list punctuation neither requires nor excludes a connective kai before Iakobos. No note is mapped here; the only note is an alternative_rendering ('Or, Jacob') about the English form of the name. Nothing in the wording distinguishes the readings.

ASV reads simply 'and Thaddaeus', with no trace of the conflate name Lebbaios or of the clause 'who was surnamed'. The RP reading Lebbaios ho epikletheis Thaddaios would have produced a second name and a surnaming clause in the English; their absence selects the bare Thaddaios.

ASV transliterates 'the Cananaean', which represents Kananaios; Kananites would give 'Canaanite', the form the older English versions used. The ASV note 'Or, Zealot' is an alternative_rendering about the sense and does not bear on the form, but the -aean spelling of the transliteration follows the base reading.

The unit is the article before the participle paradous. ASV renders 'who also betrayed him' with a relative clause, which the articular participle and the anarthrous participle in apposition both yield identically in English. Both notes are alternative_rendering and neither is mapped to this unit.

ASV prints 'raise the dead' in the commission, without brackets or a note questioning it. The RP reading omits nekrous egeirete entirely, which would leave no English for that clause; its presence selects the base.

ASV reads 'nor staff', a singular, matching rhabdon; the RP plural rhabdous would give 'nor staves', as it does in the parallel where the plural stands. The number is visible in the English and selects the base.

The variant adds the copula estin to 'the laborer is worthy of his food'. English requires 'is' whether or not the Greek expresses the verb, so the ASV wording cannot show which reading stood. No note is mapped here.
pros hymas and eph' hymas both yield 'return to you' after a verb of returning; ASV's preposition choice is governed by English idiom, not by which Greek preposition was read. No note is mapped here.
an and ean are interchangeable in the indefinite relative construction and both give ASV's 'And whosoever shall not receive you'. The English carries no mark of the difference.

ASV's 'as ye go forth out of that house or that city' renders exerchomenoi with a genitive; the compound verb alone supplies 'out of' in English, so the added exo leaves no separate word. Nothing in the wording shows whether it was read.
Aorist paradosin and present paradidosin subjunctive both render as ASV's 'when they deliver you up'; English has no form here that distinguishes the aspect after 'when'. No note is mapped.
Subjunctive lalesete and future lalesete are both rendered 'what ye shall speak' in a deliberative indirect question; the ASV 'shall speak' fits either. No note is mapped.

ASV renders 'flee into the next', an idiomatic rendering that neither heteran ('the other') nor allen ('another') is uniquely responsible for; the ASV did not translate the pronoun distinction here. No note is mapped to this unit.

The unit is the article before Israel in 'the cities of Israel'. English proper names take no article, and ASV's definite 'the cities' answers to the article on poleis, not to tou Israel. The reading is invisible in the English.
heos an elthe and heos elthe both give ASV's 'till the Son of man be come'; the modal particle has no separate English exponent. No note is mapped.

ASV reads 'If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub'. The compound epekalesan and the simplex ekalesan both fall together in 'have called'; ASV did not render the compound with 'surnamed', so no English word separates the readings. The two notes here are greek_gloss and do not bear on the verb.

Present imperative phobeisthe and aorist subjunctive phobethete after me both give ASV's prohibition 'be not afraid of them that kill the body'; English marks no such aspectual difference. The only note is a greek_gloss on Gehenna.
In the positive command ASV reads 'but rather fear him'; phobeisthe and the aorist imperative phobethete are both rendered by the bare imperative 'fear'. Nothing in the English distinguishes them.

The variant adds the article before psychen in 'both soul and body'. ASV renders the nouns anarthrously as an English idiom for the pair, so the presence or absence of the Greek article leaves no trace.
The variant adds the article before soma in 'both soul and body'. As with the parallel noun, ASV's anarthrous English pairing does not show whether the article stood.
phobeisthe and phobethete after me both give ASV's 'Fear not therefore'; the prohibition reads the same in English whichever form stood. No note is mapped.

The unit is the article in en (tois) ouranois. ASV reads 'my Father who is in heaven', which supplies neither the article nor the Greek plural, so the reading is invisible. The two notes here are greek_gloss on 'in me' and 'in him'.
hostis d' an arnesetai and hostis de arnesetai both yield ASV's 'But whosoever shall deny me'; English 'whosoever shall' covers the indefinite relative with or without an. No note is mapped.

The unit is the order of kago and auton. ASV's 'him will I also deny' fronts the object for emphasis as English idiom and matches its own 'him will I also confess' in v. 32; the arrangement is the translators' English, not a witness to Greek order.
The unit is the article in en (tois) ouranois. ASV again reads 'my Father who is in heaven', rendering neither the article nor the plural, so nothing distinguishes the readings.
an and ean are equivalent in the indefinite relative clause and both give ASV's 'And whosoever shall give to drink'. The English shows no difference.
